item.title: Everything Is a Plugin: Building on DeepSeek Harness
item.description: A hands-on walkthrough of an agent harness where every capability — the model, the tools, even the agent loop — is a swappable plugin.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR — DeepSeek Harness (dsh) is an open-source agent harness built on the "everything-is-a-plugin" idea. There is no locked-in core: the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log, and the agent loop are all plugins you can swap, replace, or extend. I ran it end-to-end with qwen3.8:27b, routed the model through LiteLLM for observability, tested a homegrown browser plugin, and poked at all four presets (Standard, PTC, Minimal, Creative). Here's what it's like, and how you'd add your own capability.

What is DeepSeek Harness?

DeepSeek Harness is, at its core, a coding agent that you can rebuild from the inside. It boots an agent, runs it over an append-only session log, and talks to a model through tools. Under the hood it is powered by a plugin framework called Cordis.

The idea that makes it different is not "an agent with a lot of tools." It's this:

There is no privileged core to patch. The model adapter, the tool registry, the session log, and the agent loop itself are all Cordis plugins mounted into one shared context. You extend the harness by mounting a new plugin beside the others — and every registration is a reversible effect that unwinds when the plugin unloads.

In other words, a "harness" here isn't a fixed product with an SDK bolted on the side. It's a composition: a tree of plugins assembled at boot, where each one registers a service on a shared context (ctx.tools, ctx.llm, ctx.agents, ctx.sessions, …) and other plugins discover that service by name instead of importing a specific implementation.

That single design choice is what makes the rest of this possible.

Getting it running

From npm:

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web

That starts a local Web UI at http://127.0.0.1:3080 and opens it in your browser.

From source:

git clone https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness.git
cd deepseek-harness
pnpm install
pnpm run build
pnpm dsh web

A running dsh boots a named profile — think of it as a saved plugin composition. The shipped ones are web (the browser app, default), headless (one-shot, no server), sdk (JSON-RPC), sdk-minimal, and acp (automation). You can even dump the exact tree your machine boots with:

dsh --profile web --dump-config

Every row it prints is a plugin you could, in principle, replace.

The part I care about most: four presets

A preset is a per-session agent composition — one file that names the tools, prompt sections, and skills a session runs with. Because each session composes independently, a single process can run several differently-shaped agents at once. Four presets ship, and they're a clean way to feel the range of what the harness can be:

Preset What it actually is
Standard The full coding agent: file editing, shell, file & web search, skills, plan mode, goals, subagents, and workflows.
PTC Standard minus the general-purpose workflow tool. Instead, the model composes multi-step work as a single TypeScript program (run_code) generated over the tool registry — several round trips collapse into one.
Minimal A fixed-prompt, two-tool agent: just a persistent shell and a str-replace editor. No skills, no plan mode, no subagents, no compaction.
Creative Standard plus the self-referential Cordis toolset and a composition-authoring skill — the preset for building other presets. Treat a session on it as shell access.

A few behaviors that surprised me in a good way:

  • The default preset is a setting — you can override it per deployment or per user.
  • A session can switch presets only while it has produced nothing. Once it's done messages or tool calls, the composition is locked for that session's life — because swapping tools mid-conversation would strand calls the new composition can't make.
  • A preset is as privileged as the plugins it names. Authoring a custom preset is a trust decision, not a cosmetic one.

My hands-on run

This is where it stopped being a read-me and became a "oh, it actually works" moment.

  • Model verified with qwen3.8:27b. Coding tasks completed cleanly. The most satisfying bit: after finishing an implementation, the agent ran tests, found its own defects, and fixed them — no errors surfaced to me.
  • Observability via LiteLLM. Because the model adapter is a plugin behind the ctx.llm seam, I routed requests through a LiteLLM gateway for tracing without touching the agent loop. That seam is a genuine observability hook, not a hack.
  • A custom browser plugin. I dropped in my own plugin and confirmed the extension path works beyond the shipped toolset.
  • All four presets exercised. Standard, PTC, Minimal, Creative — to confirm the per-session composition behaves exactly as the docs claim.

The takeaway: the harness is honest about what it is. When the model, the tools, and the loop are all the same kind of thing (a plugin), "extending it" stops being a special integration and becomes just composition.

Adding your own capability (a plugin)

A plugin is a TypeScript module that contributes something to the shared context. The most common shape is a function named apply that takes a Cordis Context:

import type { Context } from '@deepseek-ai/cordis'

export const name = 'my-plugin'          // optional label used in diagnostics

export function apply(ctx: Context) {
  // By the time this runs, everything you declared in `inject` is ready.
  console.log('[my-plugin] loaded')
}

You list the plugin in a cordis.yml (a list of entries; name is a module specifier — an npm package or a path):

- name: '/absolute/path/to/my-plugin/src/plugin.ts'

A conventional layout is my-plugin/src/plugin.ts.

Declaring dependencies

If your plugin needs a capability — the tool registry, the LLM adapter, the agent registry — say so with inject. Cordis then holds your plugin pending until that service exists, so you never see half-initialized state, and load order in the file stops mattering (dependencies decide order, not line position):

export const name = 'my-tool-plugin'
export const inject = ['tools']          // or ['tools', 'llm'], etc.

For a capability you might need, probe instead of requiring: ctx.get('tools').

Three shapes, one idea

  1. Function — the apply(ctx) form above. Use this first.
  2. Object — an object with a name, inject, and an apply method.
  3. Class / Service — when you need to expose a service that other plugins consume.
import { Service, type Context } from '@deepseek-ai/cordis'

declare module '@deepseek-ai/cordis' {
  interface Context { myService: MyService }   // compile-time typing
}

export class MyService extends Service {
  static inject = ['tools']

  constructor(ctx: Context) {
    super(ctx, 'myService')                    // register under 'myService'
    // Synchronous init here. From now on, ctx.myService works everywhere.
  }
}

The declare module block is TypeScript declaration merging — it adds myService to Context so ctx.myService type-checks. It generates no code; without it the service still works at runtime, you just lose type safety.

Getting it into a running harness

The fastest path is a one-off patch overlay — no rebuild, no permanent change:

pnpm dsh web --patch ./my-plugin/cordis.yml

A patch can replace an existing row (target it by id, swap its whole config) or insert new rows. Custom profiles reload these live, so you can iterate a plugin without restarting the whole app.

# Insert a new plugin into the running composition
- insert:
    - id: my-plugin
      name: '/absolute/path/to/my-plugin/src/plugin.ts'

# Or replace the config of an existing row (by id)
- id: webserver
  config:
    host: 127.0.0.1
    port: 3081

Cleanup

Because registrations are reversible effects, Cordis automatically unwinds what your plugin registered when the plugin unloads. If you open a resource and want it closed on teardown, register the cleanup:

export function apply(ctx: Context) {
  const socket = openThing()
  ctx.effect(() => socket.close())   // runs when this plugin unloads
}

One trust note

A plugin is as privileged as the services it touches. A row that publishes a service into the root realm is process-global; if only one agent should see it, it belongs inside an isolated realm. Treat a plugin that can read or mount the live runtime the same way you'd treat shell access — which is exactly how the harness' own Creative preset puts it.

Why I think this model matters

Most agent platforms hand you a strong, fixed agent and an SDK for the seams. The "everything is a plugin" stance inverts that: the agent is the plugin composition, so there is no "the agent" to upgrade against a vendor. Want a different model? Swap the adapter. Want a lean two-tool agent for a sandboxed context? Pick a preset. Want a capability that doesn't exist? Write ~30 lines of TypeScript and mount it.

That's not a feature list — it's a different relationship with the tool. For anyone who's ever wanted to understand and reshape the thing doing their coding, that's the interesting part.

Get started

  • Run it: npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web
  • Source: https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness
  • Cordis primer (the framework under dsh): docs/cordis-primer.md
  • Cordis tutorial (plugins, services, events, config): docs/cordis-tutorial/
  • Architecture (profiles, bundles, patches): docs/architecture.md

DeepSeek Harness is in developer preview and iterating rapidly — expect compatibility-breaking changes.
